Case study 01BeautyHomepage auditIndependent concept project

4AM Skincare — the sale arrives before the product

4amskin.com · Homepage · Desktop 1280×900 · Captured 23 Nov 2026 · Chapter of the 4AM Skincare independent CRO audit — 7 findings

4AM Skincare sells Clean Sheets — serum-infused cleansing wipes — alongside serums and bundles. This page is the homepage chapter of my full independent audit; every claim below was re-checked against the live site on capture day before publishing.

Finding 01 — the hero sells only the sale

The audit flagged a hero that never explains the product; capture day made it literal. The first screen is a full-screen sale gate — and behind it, the headline is still the sale. No supporting sentence, no benefits, no "what is this". A first-time visitor still can't tell Clean Sheets from ordinary makeup wipes.

Finding 02 — no customer proof visible on the first screen

4AM has real proof: a 4.7 buyer rating, press quotes, reported customer results. None of it touches the first screen. The press strip sits after the hero, and the customer-proof sections ("Proof not just promises", "The people have spoken") sit below the bestsellers — reassurance arrives after you've been asked to shop.

Finding 03 — bestsellers before reassurance

Page order on capture day: sale gate → sale hero → press strip → best sellers → proof sections. The audit's point stands exactly: visitors are invited to buy before they've been given a reason to believe.

Design decisions

Keep the headline; add the audit's supporting sentence — serum-infused wipes that remove makeup, sunscreen and daily buildup while leaving skin hydrated — with a clear "Shop Clean Sheets" button. Demote the offer to a slim bar and a hero sub-line; remove the entry gate. Trust line directly under that button (units sold + the 4.7 rating), then one compact proof band before the bestsellers — not a new wall of content.

Expected impact

More first-time visitors reaching the bestsellers with a reason to trust — expected effects on clicks on the main shopping button and on how far visitors scroll. Labeled honestly: expectations, not measured lifts. None of this is measured until it runs on the real store.

What this demonstrates: first impressions, which message gets the most attention, trust, and how visitors move from the homepage towards buying.

Case study 02BeautyClean Sheets product-page auditIndependent concept project

4AM Clean Sheets product page — make the easy purchase the obvious one

4amskin.com/products/clean-sheets · Desktop 1280×900 + mobile 375×812 · Captured 23 Nov 2026 · Chapter of the 4AM Skincare independent CRO audit — 7 findings

Same audit, one level deeper: the Clean Sheets product page, where a $23 decision gets complicated. Four of the audit's seven findings live on product pages — the three below land on the buy button, and the fourth, from the Routine Bundle page, is documented here with its own evidence. Everything was re-verified against the live site on capture day.

Finding 04 — the subscription maze

Monthly, quarterly and one-time purchases, each with its own price, savings and delivery arrangement to compare before you can buy — the audit rated this medium-high priority, and capture day confirmed it: three plans, plus a pre-selected button showing $55.20 against a $23.00 page price. That $55.20 is not a pricing error — the 90-day supply plan is pre-selected, and the button's total is its math: 3 packs × $18.40 (the $23.00 pack price minus 20%) = $55.20, with the quantity already set to 3. The math holds; the presentation doesn't — the button never shows the calculation, so a first-time buyer can't reconstruct it. Someone who just wants to try the wipes has to reconcile four numbers first.

Finding 05 — reviews too far from the button

The product earns a 4.7 rating, but the review content sits about 3,400px below the add-to-cart button on desktop and about 4,600px below it on mobile — both measured from the button; on a 375×812 phone screen that's nearly six screens of scrolling. For a $23 product customers may buy without much consideration, the reassurance arrives after the decision is over.

Finding 06 — promise vs expectations

"Your entire skincare routine in a wipe" is great marketing and a literal trap — buyers may expect one wipe to replace every step. The page needs to state exactly what the wipes do: cleanse, remove makeup and sunscreen, hydrate — while keeping the catchy headline.

Finding 07 — the Routine Bundle page disagrees with itself

The audit's last finding, verified live on the Routine Bundle product page: the usage sections say "apply 2-3 drops of the RISE serum" and "apply 2–3 drops of Rest" — while the Rest sections themselves say "Apply 2-3 pumps to cleansed skin" (twice), and the marketing copy promises "Two to three pumps each". Drops or pumps, a customer shouldn't have to guess how to use what they bought. The audit's fix: one consistent application guide, shown for the morning and evening routine. This finding ships as a prioritized fix rather than a redesign concept — the audit deliberately concentrates the redesign work on the two highest-impact pages.

Design decisions

Make buying once the default option. Show subscription savings, delivery frequency and cancellation terms together, so customers can compare their options without searching around — without punishing people who just want to buy once. The add-to-cart always shows the price of what's selected. Rating and review count beside the product name; one or two reviews with customer photos near the button, the full review wall further down for those who want it. On mobile, a purchase button that stays visible as customers scroll.

Expected impact

Fewer hesitations between landing and buying — we'd expect more visitors to add the product to their cart, while making subscription options easier to understand and choose. Labeled honestly: expectations, not measured lifts.

What this demonstrates: product pages, purchase friction, and using trust signals to support buying decisions.

Case study 03SuncareHome, Shop, Product page & CartIndependent auditIndependent concept project

Dune Suncare — the sale leads, the products hide behind it

dunesuncare.com · Homepage, Shop, Mineral Melt product page & Cart · Mobile 375×812, captured mobile-first · Captured 24 Nov 2026 · Second independent audit, 7 findings

Dune Suncare is a real mineral-suncare brand — about ten products including the Mineral Melt, the Lifeguard and the Mug Guard. This is my second full independent audit, covering the whole path from homepage to cart, captured mobile-first at 375×812 — the screen most shoppers actually bring. Every claim and measurement below was re-checked against the live site on capture day (24 Nov 2026).

Dune finding 1 — the hero sells the sale, not the suncare

The first screen is a pie: on-brand as a joke ("DUNE-R is served"), off-brand as an argument. Nothing in it tells a first-time visitor what Dune sells, who it's for, or why it's better — the "Clinically-proven. Derm-approved." claims are the only support, and they're unverified self-praise. The 4.7★ rating earned from 82 reviews never touches this screen — on mobile it first appears about 5,000px down.

Dune finding 2 — one product per screen, but the range stays hidden

The homepage walks one product at a time — Mineral Melt, Lifeguard, Mug Guard — with benefit lines and a quick Add to Bag. What's missing is the middle: no link to the product page, no stars, no proof, and no sign of the other seven products. On mobile it compounds: the burger menu hides the entire range, and three full-screen sections stack before any alternative appears. A visitor either buys blind or leaves.

Dune finding 3 — the product page buries what makes it different

The Mineral Melt earns 4.7★ from 82 reviews with 97% would-recommend — and on mobile the stars don't even reach the first screen: the buy controls render first (button ~595px, stars ~1,000px), and the reviews start ~5,260px down, roughly 4,700px below the button (all measured on capture day). Vegan, reef-compliant, non-nano and cruelty-free are real and verified, but they sit as bullets 4–7 of an 11-item Features list ~1,540px down — not badges anywhere near the decision.

Dune finding 4 — technical blocks compete with plain benefits

Benefits, Attributes and Features are useful — but they're unscannable plain bullets, and the page's own hierarchy buries them: Drug Facts at ~1,850px, the full ingredient list at ~2,770px, and ingredient stories scattered between. On a phone, where each screen is precious, the science crowds out the selling. The science is a strength; presented like this, it reads as homework.

Dune finding 5 — the shipping truth lives in a marquee

A customer spending $29.95 is only $15.05 away from free shipping, but the cart never tells them. That information is hidden in the announcement bar instead of appearing where it could actually encourage another purchase — the bar flashes "Free shipping on orders $45+" past as decoration, while the cart itself offers only "Taxes and shipping calculated at checkout".

Dune finding 6 — shop cards start well, then stop

Credit where due: the Shop cards carry stars, review counts, a one-line description and quick add — a real head start. But the counts are thin where they matter (the Melt Stick shows 5.0★ from 2 reviews) and the card stops there: no benefit points, no "who it's for", nothing about what makes it different. On mobile, where one card owns the screen, that's the whole pitch — and reviews alone can't tell a visitor whether a product fits them.

Dune finding 7 — three prices for one tube, in one session

Found while verifying the buy block: the Mineral Melt shows $29.95 one-time, $26.95 with the pre-selected subscription — and the cart line then displays $20.97 under the sitewide 30% code. Customers see three different prices for the same product, without a clear explanation of how they relate. Consistent pricing helps customers trust the store — and this is the kind of detail that quietly erodes that trust.

Design decisions

One quick scroll on a phone that explains the brand before it sells the sale — headline, verified trust row (4.7★ · 82 reviews · 97%), product-first hero card, and a swipeable range strip so all ten products are one swipe away instead of behind the burger. Product page: stars and the 97% stat tied to the decision; benefits as icon bullets in plain language; Vegan/reef/non-nano promoted from fine print to badges near the buy block; Drug Facts kept but demoted. One-time purchase as the default with the subscription's terms beside it; an Add to Bag that stays visible while scrolling, always showing the selected price. The real $45+ threshold surfaced in the buy flow and as a cart progress bar. Shop cards: add "who it's for" and one thing that makes each product different, with thin review counts given context.

Expected impact

A first-time visitor can understand the brand, see the range and trust the product before the ask — expected effects on taps on the main shopping button, how far visitors scroll on the product page, and how many visitors add to cart; the shipping progress bar targets more completed checkouts. Labeled honestly: expectations, not measured lifts.

What this demonstrates: the steps customers take before buying, across the whole store — which message gets the most attention, how product information is organized, consistent pricing, and showing how close someone is to free shipping.
